readingInstruction: Read Psalm 107:1-22. It begins Book 5 of the Psalter, and it is a song for the redeemed, those gathered from the lands. Notice the refrain that repeats in each scene.
settingTheScene: Psalm 107 opens the last book of the Psalms. It has no author but clearly looks back on the return from exile: “those he redeemed from trouble and gathered in from the lands.” The psalm tells four stories of people in distress: wanderers, prisoners, the sick, and sailors. The first three are in today’s reading. The psalm appears several times in this plan, with different parts. Here read it as a thanksgiving song for those who know what it is to be rescued.
observation: “Oh give thanks to the LORD, for he is good, for his steadfast love endures forever!” (v. 1).
“Let the redeemed of the LORD say so, whom he has redeemed from trouble and gathered in from the lands” (vv. 2-3).
“Some wandered in desert wastes… hungry and thirsty, their soul fainted within them” (vv. 4-5).
“Then they cried to the LORD in their trouble, and he delivered them from their distress” (v. 6).
“Some sat in darkness and in the shadow of death, prisoners in affliction and in irons” (v. 10).
“He brought them out of darkness and the shadow of death, and burst their bonds apart” (v. 14).
“Some were fools through their sinful ways… they drew near to the gates of death” (vv. 17-18).
“He sent out his word and healed them, and delivered them from their destruction” (v. 20).
interpretation:
The psalm follows a pattern in each of its stories. First, people are in trouble: lost, imprisoned, sick, or at sea. Second, they cry to the LORD in their trouble. Third, he delivers them. And fourth, a refrain: “Let them thank the LORD for his steadfast love, for his wondrous works to the children of men.” The repetition teaches us to see all rescue as grace.

The first group are wanderers. They are lost in the desert, hungry, with no city to dwell in. The exiles, scattered across Babylon, would have recognized themselves. God leads them by a straight way to a city to live in. The second are prisoners. They sit in darkness because they rebelled against the words of God. Their bondage is a result of sin. Yet when they cry, he breaks the doors of bronze and cuts the bars of iron. The third are the sick, “fools through their sinful ways,” who suffer affliction because of their iniquities. And again, when they cry, “he sent out his word and healed them.”

Notice the phrase, “He sent out his word and healed them.” The word of God is the instrument of healing. It reminds us of creation, where God spoke, and of the gospel, where Jesus speaks and the sick are healed.

Who are the redeemed? The psalm says: everyone who has been in distress and cried out. Not only Israel, but “the children of men.” Redemption in the Bible is not for the strong or the clean, but for those who cry.

The psalm ends this part with an invitation to offer thank offerings and “tell of his deeds in songs of joy.” Gratitude is the right response to rescue.
connection: Matthew 8:5-13 shows Jesus healing the centurion’s servant with a word, as in verse 20. Luke 4:18 says Jesus came to proclaim liberty to the captives. Colossians 1:13 says God “has delivered us from the domain of darkness and transferred us to the kingdom of his beloved Son.” Ephesians 2:1-5 speaks of being dead in trespasses and made alive. Acts 16:25-26 shows prison doors opened as Paul and Silas prayed.
application:
Think about which of the four pictures fits your story: wanderer, prisoner, sick, or sailor. Thank God for his rescue.

Say the refrain aloud: “Let them thank the LORD for his steadfast love.”

Tell someone a story of God’s rescue in your life this week.
prayerPrompts: Give thanks to God for a way he has redeemed you from adversity.
Thank him that his steadfast love endures forever.
Tell him whom you want to share this thanks with.
